findings.statement: Reported gross margin percentage did not widen this year: it decreased three basis points, though it rose 10 basis points excluding gasoline price inflation.
findings.rationale: The filing's own headline measure fell slightly (11.09% vs 11.12%), which is not a noticeable widening. Only the gasoline-adjusted measure rose.

quotes.text: Gross margin percentage decreased three basis points. Excluding the impact of gasoline price inflation on net sales, gross margin percentage was 11.22%, an increase of 10 basis points.

findings.statement: Margin in core merchandise categories, measured on their own sales, increased 15 basis points across all categories.
findings.rationale: If 'merchandise markup' means core merchandise margin, there was a widening, but 15 basis points is modest and the claim's 'noticeably' is not clearly met. The filing does not call the change significant.

quotes.text: The gross margin in core merchandise categories when expressed as a percentage of their own sales increased 15 basis points. The increase was across all categories.

findings.statement: The XBRL-derived annual gross margin was 12.8% in both fiscal 2026 and fiscal 2025, so it shows no widening.
findings.rationale: The backend figure uses a different basis from the filing's 11.09% merchandise gross margin, so it is a weak check, but it is flat year over year.

response.rationale: The claim is mostly challenged. The overall gross margin percentage fell three basis points. A widening appears only after excluding gasoline (up 10 basis points) or within core merchandise (up 15 basis points), and neither is large. The result depends on how 'merchandise markup' is defined.
unknowns: Whether 'merchandise markup' means total gross margin, gross margin excluding gasoline, or core merchandise margin.
What size of change the thesis counts as 'noticeable'.
How the XBRL gross margin of 12.8% is defined, and why it differs from the 11.09% in the MD&A table.
